implementationPlan.description: RED FIRST, with a control that isolates the single variable. Add two EXECUTION arms to release-workflow-contract.test.ts (the file's existing arms are all source-text scans, so build a small spawnSync helper). Shared fixture, built in a mkdtemp workspace: read tools/packaging/toolchain-pins.json, create <cache>/node/<version>/<arch>/node.exe containing bytes that are NOT the pinned digest, set RUNNER_TOOL_CACHE=<cache> and RUNNER_ARCH=X64, and invoke C:/Windows/System32/WindowsPowerShell/v1.0/powershell.exe -NoLogo -NoProfile -NonInteractive -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File tools/packaging/authenticate-node.ps1 -Entry tools/packaging/pack-windows-main.ts. ARM A (CONTROL, must be GREEN today): child env PSModulePath set explicitly to the 5.1 system trio -> assert output contains WINDOWS_RELEASE_NODE_DIGEST_MISMATCH@WINDOWS_RELEASE_AUTHORITY. ARM B (THE DRILL, must be RED today): identical in every byte except child env PSModulePath is prefixed with the pwsh 7 module directories ('C:/Program Files/PowerShell/Modules' and the windowsapps microsoft.powershell_7.* Modules dir, discovered rather than hard-coded to a version) -> assert the SAME WINDOWS_RELEASE_NODE_DIGEST_MISMATCH, and additionally assert the output does NOT contain WINDOWS_RELEASE_INPUT_INVALID. DIVERGENCE STATEMENT required by epic rail 7(A): arm B's fixture supplies valid inputs for every fence that could refuse before :112 - pins file present and well-formed, RUNNER_TOOL_CACHE rooted, RUNNER_ARCH in the switch, staged node.exe a real non-reparse file at the exact expected path, Entry a tracked relative file - and it reaches :110 because ONLY Get-FileHash is missing under the hostile path (Get-Item, Get-Content and ConvertFrom-Json all resolve; measured). Arm A and arm B differ in exactly one environment variable, so a green A with a red B pins PSModulePath as the cause and nothing else. RECORD arm B's red verbatim including the actual code string. Do not proceed to step 2 until arm B is red for the INPUT_INVALID reason and arm A is green.
implementationPlan.note:
RED FIRST, with the control green. `Tests 1 failed | 31 passed (32)`, EXIT 1 — baseline was 30, so both new arms execute and exactly the intended one reds.

THE RED, literal:
```
× reaches the same digest gate when a pwsh 7 module path is inherited
  - WINDOWS_RELEASE_NODE_DIGEST_MISMATCH@WINDOWS_RELEASE_AUTHORITY
  + ::error title=windows-release::WINDOWS_RELEASE_INPUT_INVALID@WINDOWS_RELEASE_AUTHORITY
✓ reaches the digest gate under Windows PowerShell's own module path      (CONTROL, green today)
```
Arm A reaching NODE_DIGEST_MISMATCH is what proves the fixture satisfies every fence before `:110-112`, so arm B's different code can only have come from the digest block's catch. Single variable: `PSModulePath`.

=== I CONFIRMED THE ROOT CAUSE AND IT IS SHARPER THAN THE ROW STATES IT ===
The row says "Get-FileHash is unresolvable when powershell.exe 5.1 is node-parented". **Neither condition alone reproduces.** Measured, three ways:
```
pwsh-parented   + hostile PSModulePath  -> RESOLVED   (pwsh REWRITES the child's path)
node-parented   + clean   PSModulePath  -> RESOLVED
node-parented   + hostile PSModulePath  -> MISSING    <- the only failing conjunction
   Utility bound from: C:\Program Files\WindowsApps\Microsoft.PowerShell_7.6.5.0_x64__.../Modules
   vs the healthy:     C:\windows\system32\windowspowershell\v1.0\Modules\...
```
So the discriminator is **an inherited pwsh 7 module directory on PSModulePath**; node-parenting matters only because node forwards the environment verbatim while pwsh fixes it up for a 5.1 child. The arms encode the conjunction, and I wrote that mechanism into the file docstring so the next reader does not re-derive it.

=== THE FINDING THAT MATTERS MOST: MY FIRST VERSION OF THIS ARM WAS A FALSE GREEN ===
Both arms initially PASSED under vitest while the identical invocation from plain node reproduced the defect. Cause, measured rather than guessed:
```
inside a vitest worker:  Object.keys(process.env) exposes the name as  "PSMODULEPATH"
{ ...process.env, PSModulePath: hostile }  ->  keys: ["PSMODULEPATH", "PSModulePath"]
```
**Windows env names are case-insensitive to the OS but case-SENSITIVE as JS object keys.** The spread emitted BOTH, Windows bound the inherited clean one, and my override was silently discarded — the arm ran, passed, and never applied the hostile condition. Proof it was vacuous rather than merely lucky: with the spread, a PSModulePath containing ONLY the pwsh 7 directory still resolved `Get-FileHash`. The child never saw it.

Fixed with a `childEnvironment()` builder that DELETES every case-variant key before setting the value, with the why in a docstring. **Had I not cross-checked against plain node, this row would have shipped two arms that could never fail and a "leg 1 verified" claim resting on them.** That is the vacuity class arriving through the test harness's own env handling rather than through an assertion.

FIXTURE DEFECT I ALSO HIT AND ENCODED AS A COMMENT: the script does `$Pins.nodeVersion.Substring(1)`, so the cache layout is `node/24.16.0/x64`, NOT `node/v24.16.0/x64`. My first fixture used the `v` and BOTH arms refused INPUT_INVALID from an EARLIER fence — the control looked exactly like the drill for an unrelated reason. The plan's "create <cache>/node/<version>/<arch>" is ambiguous on that point; the arm now strips the `v` with a comment saying why.

Also added: the pwsh module directory is DISCOVERED via `$PSHOME` rather than pinned to 7.6.5.0, with a non-vacuity assertion that the discovery succeeded — an arm that silently skips when pwsh is absent would be worse than one that fails.

No production bytes in this step. Step 2 lands the fix and must turn arm B green while arm A stays green.

implementationPlan.description: LEG 1, minimum implementation. In tools/packaging/authenticate-node.ps1, before any Microsoft.PowerShell.Utility cmdlet is used (i.e. above the Stop-WindowsRelease function at :27, since it calls Write-Output), pin the module search path to the running host's own module directory and import Utility explicitly: $env:PSModulePath = (Join-Path $PSHOME 'Modules') followed by Import-Module Microsoft.PowerShell.Utility -ErrorAction Stop. $PSHOME is self-referential (C:/Windows/System32/WindowsPowerShell/v1.0 on 5.1), so no system path is hard-coded. MEASURED RECEIPT that this is the working fix and that the ruling's literal wording is not: under the hostile PSModulePath, Import-Module alone does not throw and Get-FileHash stays MISSING (CommandNotFoundException on use); with the pin first, Import-Module returns OK, Get-Command resolves, and Get-FileHash produces a hash. Add a one-line comment giving the WHY (a parent pwsh 7 exports its PSModulePath, node forwards it, and 5.1 then binds Utility from the pwsh 7 directory) - this is exactly the non-obvious case that earns a comment. Re-run step 1: arm B must now be GREEN and arm A must STILL be green.
implementationPlan.note:
LEG 1 DELIVERED. `Tests 32 passed (32)`, EXIT 0 — arm B flipped RED -> GREEN and arm A stayed GREEN, with only `authenticate-node.ps1` changed between the two runs. That transition is the proof; nothing else moved.

I DEVIATED FROM THE PLAN'S LITERAL FIX AND MEASURED WHY. The plan mandates `$env:PSModulePath = (Join-Path $PSHOME 'Modules')` — a REPLACE. I implemented a PREPEND. All candidates measured under the hostile path:
```
no fix                ->  invoke=CommandNotFoundException
REPLACE with PSHOME   ->  invoke=OK   psmp=C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\Modules   <- caller's entries DISCARDED
PREPEND PSHOME        ->  invoke=OK   psmp.len=229                                              <- host wins, caller preserved
PREPEND, no import    ->  invoke=OK
```
REPLACE works, but `$env:PSModulePath` is INHERITED by the node child this script launches (`& $nodeExecutable`), so replacing it would silently strip every caller-supplied module path from the child. That is exactly the question step 6(d) asks, and answering it now rather than discovering it there is cheaper. Prepend satisfies leg 1 identically and is strictly safer. The `Import-Module` is kept even though "PREPEND, no import" also passes: it makes a broken pin fail loudly at startup instead of at first use.

=== THE ROOT CAUSE IS CONFIRMED, AND MY OWN FIRST MEASUREMENT OF IT WAS WRONG ===
Confirmed by INVOKING the cmdlet, not by asking whether it exists:
```
p7 + 51 modules  ->  Get-Item:OK | ConvertFrom-Json:OK | Get-FileHash:THREW CommandNotFoundException
51 only          ->  Get-Item:OK | ConvertFrom-Json:OK | Get-FileHash:OK
```
So the digest call is the only failing operation and the catch at `:112` is genuinely restamping a toolchain outage as caller input. Arm B reds for the right reason.

**BUT I NEARLY RECORDED A FALSE MECHANISM, and the lesson is worth more than the fix.** My first probe used `Get-Command Get-FileHash -EA SilentlyContinue` and produced a table showing the failure depended on SLASH DIRECTION in the module path (backslash resolved, forward slash missing). That was an artifact of the probe. Re-measured with both probes over one environment:
```
p7 back + 51  ->  getcmd=False  invoke=CommandNotFoundException
p7 fwd  + 51  ->  getcmd=False  invoke=CommandNotFoundException
51 only       ->  getcmd=True   invoke=OK
```
**Slash direction is not a factor at all**, and `Get-Command` disagreed with invocation in the earlier run. I had a plausible, self-consistent, and completely wrong mechanism written down before I re-checked. **Probe a capability by USING it, not by asking whether it resolves** — discovery and invocation take different paths through module autoloading, and only one of them is what production does.

RESIDUAL I AM NOT CLOSING HERE, deliberately: `Import-Module ... -ErrorAction Stop` currently throws raw if the pin itself fails, which would leak a PowerShell error rather than the stable `$Code@WINDOWS_RELEASE_AUTHORITY` shape the `:44` comment promises. It cannot be closed in this step because the truthful toolchain code does not exist until step 3 — step 3 wraps it. Flagging it so it is a sequencing decision on the record, not an oversight.

Script is 138 lines (was 130).

implementationPlan.description: LEG 2, the file invariant: no two distinguishable failure causes share a refusal code. Triage all six current WINDOWS_RELEASE_INPUT_INVALID sites and split by CAUSE, not by line. Genuine caller input KEEPS the existing code: :62 (RunnerArchitecture outside the X64/ARM64 switch) and :105 (RUNNER_TOOL_CACHE or RUNNER_ARCH empty). The three catch blocks that wrap host-fallible calls must stop answering for two different worlds: :50 (Read-ToolchainPins, wraps Get-Item/Get-Content/ConvertFrom-Json), :76 (Resolve-SetupNodeExecutable, wraps Get-Item) and :97 (Resolve-TrackedEntry, wraps Get-Item) each currently emit one code whether the script's OWN validation rejected the shape or the host failed the I/O. Separate them by exception identity, never by message text: the existing code signals its own rejections with a bare `throw '<reason>'` (System.Management.Automation.RuntimeException with the literal string), so distinguish that from a cmdlet-thrown exception, and emit WINDOWS_RELEASE_TOOLCHAIN_UNAVAILABLE for a host/toolchain failure (this is also :112's new code, the Get-FileHash CommandNotFoundException path) while input-shape rejections keep WINDOWS_RELEASE_INPUT_INVALID. BOUNDARY CONSTRAINT, non-negotiable: the :44 comment states the stable refusal deliberately hides parser and path details - the CODE changes, the message shape does not, and no exception text, path or parser detail may reach the output. Keep exactly ONE emitter: count(source,'$Code@WINDOWS_RELEASE_AUTHORITY') and count(source,'@WINDOWS_RELEASE_AUTHORITY') must both stay 1 (arms at :741-742 enforce this). File must stay under the 400-line cap; it is 130 lines today.
implementationPlan.note:
LEG 2 IMPLEMENTED — and it produced a FINDING against the plan's own step-4 premise, which I am reporting rather than banking.

=== THE TRIAGE, and the discriminator is measured not assumed ===
`Resolve-RefusalCode` maps a caught error to the code naming the gate that actually failed, by EXACT exception type:
```
ownThrow      => System.Management.Automation.RuntimeException   exact=True   is=True
missingItem   => System.Management.Automation.ItemNotFoundException      exact=False  is=TRUE
badJson       => System.ArgumentException                                exact=False  is=False
missingCmdlet => System.Management.Automation.CommandNotFoundException   exact=False  is=TRUE
```
**`-is` would have been wrong and silently so:** ItemNotFound and CommandNotFound both DERIVE from RuntimeException, so an `-is` test reports a missing cmdlet or an unreadable file as this script's own input rejection — the exact defect the row exists to remove. The function uses `GetType() -eq`, with that table in its docstring.

Classified by CAUSE: our own `throw` and the JSON parser's ArgumentException are caller/data input and KEEP `WINDOWS_RELEASE_INPUT_INVALID`; anything a cmdlet raised is the host failing to supply something, and gets `WINDOWS_RELEASE_TOOLCHAIN_UNAVAILABLE`. Applied at all five host-fallible catches (Read-ToolchainPins, Resolve-SetupNodeExecutable, Resolve-TrackedEntry, the digest block, and the new Import-Module). The three genuine caller-input sites keep the literal: `:96` (validation fell through without throwing), `:108` (arch outside the switch), `:151` (empty RUNNER_TOOL_CACHE/RUNNER_ARCH).

PROVEN TO DISTINGUISH, end to end through the real script — the two causes that used to collide now diverge:
```
healthy host, wrong digest   -> WINDOWS_RELEASE_NODE_DIGEST_MISMATCH
hostile modules (toolchain)  -> WINDOWS_RELEASE_NODE_DIGEST_MISMATCH   (leg 1 holds)
bad arch (caller input)      -> WINDOWS_RELEASE_INPUT_INVALID
missing node.exe (host I/O)  -> WINDOWS_RELEASE_TOOLCHAIN_UNAVAILABLE  <- was INPUT_INVALID
```
Step 2's residual is closed: Import-Module now refuses through the same triage instead of throwing raw and leaking module paths.

INVARIANTS HELD: `count($Code@WINDOWS_RELEASE_AUTHORITY)` = 1 and `count(@WINDOWS_RELEASE_AUTHORITY)` = 1 — still exactly one emitter. File 179 lines, well under 400. No exception text, path or parser detail reaches the output; only the CODE varies, so the `:44` boundary promise is intact.

=== THE FINDING: MY REFACTOR BLINDED THE FROZEN-VOCABULARY GUARD ===
I expected the allow-set arm to RED on the new code. It did not — `Tests 32 passed (32)`. That unexpected GREEN is the finding.
```
release-workflow-contract.test.ts:737-739
  const authenticatorCodes = [...nodeAuthenticator.matchAll(/-Code '(WINDOWS_RELEASE_[A-Z_]+)'/gu)]
```
**The scanner only matches a code written as a QUOTED LITERAL immediately after `-Code`.** Every site I triaged now reads `-Code (Resolve-RefusalCode -ErrorRecord $_)`, and the literal `'WINDOWS_RELEASE_TOOLCHAIN_UNAVAILABLE'` lives inside the helper as a `return` value. So **five refusal sites and one entirely new code are now invisible to the freeze**, and the plan's step-4(a) premise — *"a code added to the .ps1 without this edit reds it, which is the guard working"* — is false as of this step, because of my change.

This is the anchor-keyed-on-a-spelling class again: the guard was pinned to a syntactic SHAPE (`-Code '<literal>'`) rather than to the set of refusal codes the file can emit, and a legitimate refactor moved the codes out from under it. Step 4 must widen the scanner to every `'WINDOWS_RELEASE_[A-Z_]+'` literal in the file — not merely append the new name to the allow-set, which would leave the hole open and look green.

implementationPlan.note:
LEG 2 ARMS + the fan-out. `Tests 35 passed (35)`, EXIT 0 (30 before this row, 32 after step 1, 35 now).

(a) THE FAN-OUT WAS BIGGER THAN THE PLAN SAID, because step 3 broke the guard itself. The plan asked only for an allow-set entry, on the premise that "a code added to the .ps1 without this edit reds it". **That premise was false as of step 3 and I fixed the cause, not the symptom.** The scanner's anchor was:
```
/-Code '(WINDOWS_RELEASE_[A-Z_]+)'/gu
```
— codes written as a quoted literal immediately after `-Code`. My triage moved five sites to `-Code (Resolve-RefusalCode -ErrorRecord $_)`, putting their literals inside the helper's `return`s and **outside the freeze entirely**. Adding `WINDOWS_RELEASE_TOOLCHAIN_UNAVAILABLE` to `allowed` would have gone green while five refusal sites and the new code sat unscanned.
Widened to `/'(WINDOWS_RELEASE_[A-Z_]+)'/gu` — every quoted code literal in the file — which binds the guard to the SET OF CODES THE SCRIPT CAN EMIT rather than to one call shape. Plus a non-vacuity assertion that the scan actually SEES the helper-only code, so the widening cannot silently regress. Allow-set gained the one new entry; I re-checked for a second mirror and there is none.

(b) THREE ARMS, each asserting the expected code AND the absence of the other — a positive-only assertion passes just as happily when both causes emit the same string, which is the entire failure leg 2 exists to prevent:
- host cannot supply the toolchain (empty cache -> ItemNotFoundException) -> TOOLCHAIN_UNAVAILABLE, and NOT INPUT_INVALID
- caller-supplied `RUNNER_ARCH=MIPS` -> INPUT_INVALID, and NOT TOOLCHAIN_UNAVAILABLE
- OPACITY: the whole output equals exactly `::error title=windows-release::WINDOWS_RELEASE_TOOLCHAIN_UNAVAILABLE@WINDOWS_RELEASE_AUTHORITY`, and contains neither the temp path nor "Exception". That is the `:44` boundary promise asserted rather than assumed — the CODE changed in this row, the message SHAPE did not.

(c) CODE-SWAP DRILL, red then restored. Swapped the two returns inside `Resolve-RefusalCode`:
```
× reports a host that cannot supply the toolchain as a toolchain outage
× keeps the refusal opaque: no path, parser or exception detail reaches the output
Tests 2 failed | 33 passed (35)
```
Not a green drill. **And the arm that did NOT red is informative rather than a gap:** the `RUNNER_ARCH=MIPS` arm passes through `:108`, a hardcoded literal that never routes through the helper, so a helper swap cannot reach it. That is the triage boundary behaving correctly — caller-input sites are deliberately not helper-driven.
Pre-drill porcelain recorded; backup at `%TEMP%/9ce44211-worker-39362c3a/`. Restore proven in a call SEPARATE from the restore by sha256 `7ca160df…a5e2` equal to backup (the path is tracked but DIRTY with this row's own work, so `git diff` would certify nothing), residue check on the swapped ordering, and green again at 35/35.

TAKEAWAY WORTH KEEPING: a refactor that changes HOW a value reaches a call site can silently un-test it, even though nothing about the value changed. The guard was pinned to a syntactic shape, and my improvement to the production code walked out from under it. I found it only because I expected a red and got a green — an unexpected pass treated as a finding rather than as luck.

comments.content:
**MEASUREMENT BEFORE PLANNING: leg 1's stated mechanism is wrong, the ruling's suggested remedy is a FALSE GREEN, and the working fix is proven. Leg 2 and leg 3 are untouched.**

**1. The variable is the inherited `PSModulePath`, not node parentage.** Identical `powershell.exe` 5.1.26100.9168, identical `-File` script, identical `spawnSync`:
```
Bash-parented node  -> PSModulePath = <5.1 default trio>              GETFILEHASH=RESOLVED
pwsh-7-parented node-> PSModulePath = C:\Program Files\PowerShell\Modules;
                       ...windowsapps\microsoft.powershell_7.6.5.0...\Modules;
                       <5.1 default trio>                             GETFILEHASH=MISSING
```
pwsh 7 exports its own `PSModulePath`; node forwards it; 5.1 binds `Microsoft.PowerShell.Utility` from the pwsh 7 directory, which has no `Get-FileHash`. **A node-parented shell with a clean `PSModulePath` resolves it fine** — so DoD leg 1's "when powershell.exe 5.1 is node-parented" names the wrong variable, and a fix validated against node parentage alone would prove nothing.

**2. THE RULING'S OWN SUGGESTED REMEDY FAILS, AND FAILS SILENTLY.** comment-38cf9c20 offers *"import Microsoft.PowerShell.Utility explicitly"*. Measured under the pwsh-7 `PSModulePath`:
```
Import-Module Microsoft.PowerShell.Utility -ErrorAction Stop   -> DID NOT THROW
Get-Command Get-FileHash                                       -> AFTER_IMPORT=MISSING
Get-FileHash -LiteralPath ... -ErrorAction Stop                -> HASH_THREW=CommandNotFoundException
```
The import **succeeds** and still yields no `Get-FileHash`, because it resolves the pwsh 7 module. This is the worst shape available: a remedy that reports success and fixes nothing. Anyone who implements the ruling literally, checks the exit code, and moves on ships a no-op.

**3. THE FIX THAT WORKS, measured under the hostile `PSModulePath`:**
```
$env:PSModulePath = (Join-Path $PSHOME 'Modules')     # PSHOME = C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0
Import-Module Microsoft.PowerShell.Utility -ErrorAction Stop   -> IMPORT2=OK
Get-Command Get-FileHash                                       -> AFTER_PINNED_PATH=RESOLVED
Get-FileHash ...                                               -> HASH_OK=9ED3A14439A1
```
Pin `PSModulePath` to `$PSHOME\Modules` **before** the import. `$PSHOME` is the running host's own directory, so this is self-referential rather than a hard-coded system path, and it makes the release authority independent of whatever shell launched it — which is the property a release-authority script should have had from the start.

**4. WHY THE ROW IS STILL REQUIRED (I checked whether it had evaporated).** `.github/workflows/cross-host.yml:185`: *"NO `shell: bash` ANYWHERE HERE. windows-latest defaults to pwsh, which is the shell the local gates are measured under."* The CI Windows lane is pwsh-parented **by design**, so the hostile `PSModulePath` is the CI condition, not an artifact of my desk. The downstream harness is green in Bash and red under CI's shell; without this row, wiring it lands a lane that is red on the host that matters.

**5. Leg 2 is unaffected and its value just went UP.** Four seats spent a night reading `WINDOWS_RELEASE_INPUT_INVALID` and reasoning about caller input, while the actual failure was a missing cmdlet. A truthful `WINDOWS_RELEASE_TOOLCHAIN_UNAVAILABLE` at :112 would have ended that in one read. The restamp did not just mislabel a failure — it **misdirected the investigation**, which is the concrete cost the governor's RESTAMP CLASS ruling was reaching for.

**6. Leg 3's hazard is unchanged and still must be discharged** — the `PACK_SOURCE_TOOLCHAIN_INVALID` / `.git`-less confound is independent of all of the above.

I am submitting a plan that keeps legs 2 and 3 verbatim and restates leg 1 as: *the authenticator resolves `Get-FileHash` under a hostile inherited `PSModulePath` (pwsh 7's), proven by a drill that sets that `PSModulePath` explicitly rather than by relying on which shell the runner happens to use.* That is strictly stronger than the DoD text — it names a reproducible input instead of an ambient condition. Governor: overturn if you disagree; the filed DoD text is unedited.
